results.title: MICE (Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations): A Step‑by‑Step Guide to Multivariate Imputation | by Pravin More | Medium
results.content: # MICE (Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations): A Step‑by‑Step Guide to Multivariate Imputation. > *Deep into* ***MICE — Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations*** *— a practical and powerful way to impute missing data when other features can help predict them.*. * **Use MICE** when your data is **MCAR** (Missing Completely at Random) or **MAR** (Missing At Random). * MICE works by **iteratively training a model per feature with missing values**, predicting the missing entries using the other features, and repeating until values **stabilize**. **MICE leverages correlations** between variables to produce more realistic imputations, often leading to better downstream model performance. Standard imputation is risky without explicitly modeling missingness. > ***Use MICE primarily for MCAR/MAR.*** *For MNAR, consider collecting more data, using indicator variables, or modeling the missingness process.*. Temporarily fill all missing cells with simple imputations (e.g., column mean) so that every model can train. import numpy as npimport pandas as pd# If your scikit-learn version requires enabling experimental:# from sklearn.experimental import enable_iterative_imputer # noqa: F401from sklearn.impute import IterativeImputerfrom sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor# Example data (X) with missing values (np.nan)X = pd.DataFrame({ 'staff_spend': [12.0, np.nan, 9.0, 11.0, np.nan], 'admin_spend': [10.0, 12.0, np.nan, 13.0, 10.0], 'marketing_spend':[30.0, 29.0, 27.0, np.nan, 28.0],})# Base estimator can be linear models, random forests, XGBoost, etc.# Choose according to your data size and relationships (linear vs nonlinear).imp = IterativeImputer( estimator=RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1), max_iter=10, # number of chained iterations initial_strategy='mean', imputation_order='ascending', # or 'roman', 'arabic', 'random' random_state=42, sample_posterior=False # True approximates multiple imputations)X_imputed = pd.DataFrame(imp.fit_transform(X), columns=X.columns)print(X_imputed) import as import as. # install.packages("mice")library(mice)df <- data.frame( staff_spend = c(12, NA, 9, 11, NA), admin_spend = c(10, 12, NA, 13, 10), marketing_spend = c(30, 29, 27, NA, 28))# m = number of multiple imputations; maxit = chained iterations per imputationimp <- mice(df, m = 5, maxit = 10, method = 'pmm', seed = 42)# Completed datasetscompleted1 <- complete(imp, 1)completed2 <- complete(imp, 2)# ...# Fit your model on each completed dataset, then pool estimates# For example, with linear regression:fit <- with(imp, lm(marketing_spend ~ staff_spend + admin_spend))pool(fit). * **Multiple imputation**: generate *m* versions, fit models on each, and **pool** metrics/coefficients (e.g., Rubin’s rules). * **MNAR**: Don’t blindly impute; consider collecting missingness indicators (`is_missing_*`) and modeling the mechanism.

results.content: 25 Types of assumptions • Presumed mechanisms of missing data – MCAR, MAR, MNAR • Analytic models involve – Analysis populations (efficacy, safety, etc.) – Distributional assumptions (mean, variance, parametric family) – Form of modeled variables (linear, dichotomized, interactions) – Auxiliary variables included in missing data models – Departures from MAR or MNAR assumptions 26 Guiding Principles • Maintain RCT / regulatory standards – Per randomization analyses – Pre-specification of analysis methods – Try for analysis obtained if no missing data occurred • Estimands, estimates, inferential methods • Avoid unnecessary assumptions – Avoid (semi)parametric assumptions across treatment arms • Minimize dimensionality of untestable assumptions – “Don’t make up 14 numbers to arrive at 1 made up number” • “Tipping point” analyses to identify limits of evidence 27 Primary Analysis • Addresses missing data: typically MAR, but perhaps MNAR – E.g., presume 30 day survival following hospital discharge • Relatively distribution-free probability model – Distribution-free interpretation of common analysis methods • Preserves weighting used in absence of missing data • Analysis method treats MAR as special case of MNAR • All of above easily addressed using multiple imputation – Also relatively transparent assumptions 28 Framework for Sensitivity Analyses • Separate MNAR parameters for each treatment arm • Assume average MNAR ”effect” across modeled baseline covariates • Tipping point analyses (using contour plots?) for p values, CI – Based on minimal parameterization of MNAR • Descriptive analyses of missing data – Exploration of stratum specific MNAR ”effects” that correspond to average MNAR ”effects” reported in tipping point analyses 29 Reporting Analyses • Devote much attention to descriptive statistics that might – Indicate the magnitude of data that had to be imputed – Support the reasoning behind particular sensitivity analyses • Descriptive statistics overall and by missingness patterns – Baseline (pre-randomization) – Treatment administered: dose delays, reductions, holidays, d/c – Patient disposition: d/c drug, d/c assessments, withdraw consent • Perhaps time to d/c or withdrawal by important predictors – Any interim measures of primary, secondary, safety outcomes • Provide primary analysis inference and summarize tipping points – Summarize how more detailed assumptions might translate to parameterizations used in sensitivity analyses 30 Example: Methotrexate in PBC • Combes, et al, Hepatology, 2005 – Issues with stopping study drug, clinic visits, or all follow-up Example: Methotrexate in PBC • Premature discontinuation of clinic visits – Missing time to subclinical progression of hyperbilirubinemia • Compare those with / without premature discontinuation – Baseline characteristics – Most recent bilirubin levels – Trends in bilirubin levels – (But interested in patterns of bilirubin after discontinuation) 31 32 Methods of Analyzing Data An Example Where am I going?

results.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Not Missing at Random - Statistical Horizons
results.content: I’m happy to report that PROC MI in SAS 9.4 has several options for doing a sensitivity analysis based on multiple imputation. LEARN MORE IN A SEMINAR WITH PAUL ALLISON There are two widely-used “modern” methods for handling missing data: multiple imputation and maximum likelihood. It’s possible to do multiple imputation or maximum likelihood when data are missing not at random (MNAR), but to do that, you first need to specify a model for the missing data mechanism—that is, a model of how missingness depends on both observed and unobserved quantities. We can, for example, specify an imputation model that says that the imputed values of GRADRAT are only 80% of what they would be if the data were actually missing at random. Here’s the SAS code for doing that: PROC MI DATA=MY.COLLEGE OUT=MIOUT; VAR GRADRAT CSAT LENROLL STUFAC PRIVATE RMBRD ACT; MNAR ADJUST(GRADRAT / SCALE=.80); This program produces five data sets, with missing data imputed by linear regression. Another option allows you to restrict the adjustments to certain subsets of the data, e.g., MNAR ADJUST(GRADRAT / SHIFT = -20 ADJUSTOBS=(PRIVATE=’1’)); This says to subtract 20 points from the imputed values of graduation rates, but only for private colleges, not for public colleges. But the SAS method is more elegant because the adjustments are made at each iteration, and the adjusted imputations are used in imputing other variables with missing data in later steps of the algorithm. 1. **Paul Allison**says: September 26, 2022 at 2:17 pm If you are concerned that your data may be not missing at random, I do think it’s worth exploring the kinds of models described by Muthen et al. Are the selection model and pattern mixture considered as multiple imputation or likelihood -based methods ? 1. **Paul Allison**says: November 19, 2015 at 5:13 pm Maximum likelihood and multiple imputation can both be used for pattern-mixture models and for selection models. Bayesian methods are likelihood-based, and the goal of multiple imputation is to make random draws from the predictive posterior distribution of the missing data given the observed data.

results.title: Unveiling the Magic of MICE: (Multiple Imputation with Chained Equations) | by Vishesh Gupta | Medium
results.content: Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) is a robust technique that addresses one specific category of missing data: Missing At Random (MAR). Before delving into the intricacies of MICE, it’s essential to understand the different categories of missing data and how MICE becomes a beacon of hope for handling MAR. 1. **Missing Completely At Random (MCAR):** In this scenario, the missingness is entirely random, and it occurs independently of both observed and unobserved variables. 2. **Missing At Random (MAR):** Missingness is categorized as MAR when the probability of a variable being missing depends on other observed variables but not on the unobserved data. In other words, although the data is missing, the reason for its absence is explained by other variables in the dataset. 3. **Missing Not At Random (MNAR):** This type of missingness occurs when the probability of missingness depends on the unobserved data itself. In MNAR situations, the missing data can introduce significant bias into your analysis, as the missingness is related to the data that’s missing. > **MICE: A Savior for Missing At Random (MAR) Data**. Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) is particularly helpful in addressing the MAR category of missing data. MICE operates under the assumption that the missing data mechanism is MAR. By leveraging these observed variables, MICE creates imputed values that align with the data’s inherent patterns. These models are constructed based on observed variables, allowing MICE to impute missing values while considering relationships within the dataset. 2. **Chained Equations:** The “chained equations” part of MICE refers to the iterative process of imputing values for each variable. 3. **Multiple Imputations:** MICE generates multiple imputed datasets, each reflecting a plausible variation of the missingness pattern. Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) shines brightest in the realm of Missing At Random (MAR) data. While MCAR and MNAR situations present their own challenges, MICE’s power lies in its ability to harness observed relationships to impute missing values, ensuring that the imputations are consistent with the dataset’s underlying patterns. By understanding the categories of missing data and embracing techniques like MICE, data analysts and researchers can confidently handle missing data scenarios, unlocking accurate insights that might have otherwise remained obscured.

results.title: How do you deal with missing not at random (MNAR) data in a clinical setting? | by NS Academy | Medium
results.content: # **How do you deal with missing not at random (MNAR) data in a clinical setting?**. Dealing with **Missing Not At Random (****MNAR****)** data in a **clinical setting** is tricky because the probability of missingness depends on the unobserved value itself — meaning you can’t just “impute and move on” like with MCAR (Missing Completely at Random) or MAR (Missing at Random). * **Sensitivity to proxies**: See if missingness correlates with observed variables (can hint at MNAR, though you can’t prove it without extra data). * **Transparency**: Always report the proportion and pattern of missing data, plus results from sensitivity analyses. * **Patient safety**: If missingness is informative about deterioration (e.g., missing vitals from ICU patients), treat it as an early warning signal, not just a data problem. Using a **pattern-mixture model** with clinical priors (assuming missing HbA1c values were likely higher), the treatment effect was smaller but still significant, helping regulators trust the robustness of the findings.
